value: Grid operators get weeks of charge stored like grain in silos, with no drying or redissolving, discharged through a cheap, large-area, slow carbon cell sized for days-long output.
estimate: Walden's rule (conductivity scales as 1/viscosity) ties the stack's conductance to the same mobility the glass freezes. A sugar melt at Tg+40 K has a viscosity of about 10^3-10^4 Pa·s (WLF), so its conductivity is about 10^-6 S/m, against about 5 S/m needed for 100 mA/cm² at 0.1 V over a 0.5 mm gap: roughly 10^6 short. Getting to about 0.5 Pa·s (about 0.01 S/m) needs about Tg+120 K. With Tg at 50°C that means about 170°C, which costs 1.6 kJ/kg·K × 145 K ≈ 64 Wh/kg of sensible heat against about 40 Wh/kg stored (1.5 mol/kg radicals per side, 2 V cell). So the heat exchanger must recover at least 90%, and the stack must be large, thin-gapped and slow, which is affordable only because discharge lasts about 100 h.

label: ED:EC:EB:g1_loop2
name: Self-mediated flushed lignin bed
anchor: lignin bed mediated by its own dissolved fragments
mech: A water-saturated bed of waste lignin is held at pH about 11, so it keeps about 0.1 M of its own quinone-bearing fragments dissolved. This pore water is slowly flushed (about 3 m/day) in a loop between the bed and a compact carbon stack with a cheap counter electrode. The fragments are charged in the stack and hand their charge to the solid lignin as they percolate, so the insulating bulk becomes active with no added chemical and no electrodes inside the bed. At about 1 mmol e⁻/g and about 0.7 V the bed holds about 9 kWh/m³, and flow paths of about 2.5 m sustain a 100-hour discharge. Occasional heavy-water charges tag the cycling quinones, and NMR on cores shows how deep each pass reaches into the grains, which sets the flow rate and bed length.
value: Pulp and biorefinery sites turn a nearly free byproduct into weeks-long storage: the bed is plain earthworks and only a small stack, sized for power, is fabricated.
estimate: Assumptions: about 1 mmol e⁻/g of native quinone sites, 500 kg lignin per m³ and a 100 h discharge. The bed must then deliver about 130 A/m³. Diffusing fragments (10 mM, effective D about 1e-10 m²/s, 2 e⁻) can supply only nFDc/L per unit area, so every grain must lie within L ≈ √(nFDc/j) ≈ 1 mm of an electrode. Electrode area scales as 1/L², so this needs about 10^6 times more electrode than "sparse buried electrodes" spaced a metre apart. Advection breaks this scaling: pore water carrying 0.1 M fragments at a Darcy flow of about 3 m/day delivers nFcu·½ ≈ 340 A/m², enough to drain about 2.5 m of bed, at about 0.1% pumping power (permeability about 1e-11 m²).

label: ED:EC:EB:g2_imm
name: Peroxide plant local reserve
anchor: merchant peroxide inventory doubling as power reserve
mech: A membraneless carbon cell array reduces air oxygen to peroxide in soda-ash solution and crystallizes sodium percarbonate. It runs as a merchant plant on cheap surplus power, selling to bleaching, water-treatment and detergent buyers at a high capacity factor. About one month of output, about 25 kt of percarbonate per 100 kt/yr plant (about 3 GWh at 0.13 kWh/kg), is held back in silos. During a dark calm spell it is discharged through the same cells back to oxygen and water, giving about 9 MW of firm power for two weeks per plant. The about 10% round-trip is acceptable only because the reserve is made from near-zero-price power and costs about $3/kWh of inventory.
value: Industrial parks hosting peroxide production get a roughly 10 MW, two-week local reserve whose converter is paid for by chemical sales: a resilience asset, not whole-grid storage.
estimate: Discharging percarbonate (2H2O2→2H2O+O2: 1.07 V ideal, about 0.5 V in practice, 1 e⁻ per H2O2) gives about 0.13 kWh/kg, so the stockpile costs only about $3/kWh at $0.4/kg. The converter's power, however, is fixed by its merchant production current. A 100 kt/yr H2O2 plant runs about 1.8e7 A, which at 0.5 V delivers only about 9 MW, and the world's entire output of about 5 Mt/yr corresponds to about 0.45 GW. That is about 20x less than one 10 GW grid needs. Discharge power scales with the size of the chemical market, not the size of the grid. Round-trip is about 10% (about 2.2 V to make, about 0.5 V back).

label: ED:EC:EB:g1_mech
name: Vapour-swing clay hydration store
anchor: energy as unmet clay hydration, fixed beds
mech: Thin swelling-clay beds sit fixed in earth-covered, vacuum-tight enclosures that only have to resist atmospheric pressure (0.1 MPa instead of about 260 MPa). Energy is stored as unmet hydration energy at about 7 Wh/kg, about 150 kg of clay per kWh, roughly $7/kWh at $50/t. To charge, one shared vapour compressor draws water vapour off one bed at a time at about 0.5 kPa (RH about 0.15) and condenses it into a pond. To discharge, pond water evaporates and expands through a low-pressure vapour turbine into the dry clay, valved from bed to bed. The adsorption heat (about 10x the work) must flow back to the pond across 3 K or less, so beds and pond are interleaved through thin walls. The machine handles about 1 m³/s of vapour per kW, so it is costly per kW and pays only at multi-week durations.
value: Grid operators get multi-week storage whose capacity costs about as much as clay earthworks and a vacuum liner, with one vapour machine, sized only for power, as the converter.
estimate: The first interlayer water is held at Δμ = RT ln(RH about 0.15) ≈ 4.7 kJ/mol ≈ 0.26 MJ per kg of water. At about 0.1 kg water per kg clay that is about 7 Wh per kg of clay, equivalent to a press pressure of Δμ/V_w ≈ 260 MPa. Any structure holding a pressure p over a volume that changes by a fraction f stores at most fσ/(1.5ρ) ≈ 0.2 × 300 MPa / (1.5 × 7850 kg/m³) ≈ 1.4 Wh per kg of steel, whatever the pressure, plate or column size. That is about 700 kg (about $700) of steel per kWh, roughly 50x the goal. 260 MPa is also the weight of about 10 km of overburden, so earth cannot carry it either.

label: ED:EC:EB:g1_loop
name: Gas-main iron feeder battery
anchor: retired gas main as iron-plating cell
mech: A retired steel or cast-iron gas main is relined with a porous separator sleeve. Its wall is the iron-plating negative electrode and current collector, and a carbon-fibre cable down the bore is the positive. A complexing agent keeps the iron-salt electrolyte near neutral pH, so the roughly 0.1 mm of iron plated per full charge neither gives off hydrogen nor eats the wall. Each metre stores about 0.4 kWh, about 120 kWh per 300 m segment, through the transformer's inverter, which earns its keep daily with peak-shaving (about 30 kW for 4 h) and voltage support. In a calm, dark spell the segment can carry only critical feeder loads (about 1.5 kW for three days: streetlights, telecom, pumps), and night-time open-circuit checks valve out segments that leak or drift.
value: Distribution utilities get daily storage plus a multi-day critical-load reserve at every street transformer with no new land or tanks, paid for by everyday feeder work, but not weeks of supply for a whole feeder.
estimate: A 150 mm main holds about 17.7 L per metre. At about 1.5 M Fe²⁺ in an all-iron couple (1.2 V, 3 Fe²⁺ per 2 e⁻) that is about 0.57 kWh/m in theory and about 0.4 kWh/m usable, so a roughly 300 m segment per street transformer stores about 120 kWh. A 100-home transformer averaging about 100 kW needs about 10-17 MWh for 4-7 days, about 100x more. Energy scales with bore area × iron solubility, so even a 600 mm main (16x the bore area) or 2 M electrolyte cannot close the gap.

label: ED:EC:EB:g1_mech
name: Electro-triggered strain heat store
anchor: strained liquid relaxing via its radical cation
mech: A neat strained liquid of the norbornadiene-quadricyclane class (about 90 kJ/mol, about 0.27 kWh of heat per kg) is charged electrochemically through a radical-anion channel where the strained form is the downhill product, and it sits inert in plain steel tanks. To discharge, it flows over a carbon-felt anode that injects a few holes, and each relaxed cation oxidizes the next strained molecule in a chain of thousands of turnovers per electron. The felt thus acts as a switchable catalyst that releases the strain as heat at about 150-200°C into an organic Rankine cycle at about 20-25%, about 60 Wh of electricity per kg. Round-trip is only about 15-20%, so this pays only if the liquid costs under about $0.5/kg (about $8/kWh) and the charging power is nearly free.
value: Grid operators get a pumpable, inert liquid whose extra days cost only tank volume, returned as dispatchable heat-to-power. It suits absorbing nearly free surplus, not efficient arbitrage.
estimate: The hole-transfer step (relaxed radical cation + strained neutral → relaxed neutral + strained radical cation) is downhill by the same roughly 0.9 eV (about 90 kJ/mol ÷ F) that would give the cell voltage, so it runs near diffusion control (k about 1e9-1e10 M⁻¹s⁻¹). Its rate depends on the abundant neutral strained molecules (about 1-10 M), not on the dilute cations, so low current density does not help. Each relaxed cation lives about 0.1-1 ns and moves about 1 nm, while reaching a cathode 100 µm downstream takes seconds: off by about 10^10. On top of that, the anode itself, held below the relaxed couple's potential, re-reduces any relaxed cation that touches it.

label: ED:EC:EB:g1_loop2
name: Earthen bipolar clay pile
anchor: excavated clay and ore beds as electrodes
mech: Excavated iron-rich smectite (layer iron switching between Fe(III) and Fe(II), about 1 mmol e⁻/g) and crushed manganese-oxide ore are laid as 3 cm layers, each mixed with about 10 vol% cheap char so every platelet is within about 2 mm of carbon. A dissolved mediator in salty pore water ferries electrons over that last distance. The layers are stacked as a bipolar earth pile: Fe-clay, a 5 mm compacted bentonite liner, MnO2 ore, then a graphite-foil sheet into the next cell. Each cell stores about 0.7 kWh per m² of sheet with about 0.07 V of ohmic loss at two-week discharge. The only fabricated parts are the about $5/m² sheets (about $7/kWh) and an inverter; everything else is earth at tens of dollars per tonne.
value: Utilities and landowners get a weeks-long store built with earthmoving and layering equipment from local clay and ore, where the electrode itself is the converter, so no stack capex sits idle.
estimate: Assumptions: about 1 mmol e⁻/g of reversible layer iron at 1500 kg/m³, giving about 1.45e8 C/m³ (about 24 kWh/m³ at 0.6 V), discharged over two weeks, so about 120 A/m³. Ionic drop through a bed of thickness H is j·H²/(2σ). With pore brine at an effective 2 S/m, keeping the drop under 0.05 V needs H ≤ √(2σΔV/j) ≈ 4 cm. Mediator reach is √(FDc/j) ≈ 2 mm (50 mM, effective D 1e-10 m²/s). So beds a metre thick fail by about 30-100x in thickness, and rods metres apart fail by far more. Thickness, not bed volume, is the controlling length.

label: ED:EC:EB:g1_mech
name: Locked-rubber bale yard
anchor: strain-crystallization-locked stretched tyre rubber
mech: Bands cut from natural-rubber-rich scrap truck tyres, screened for strain fixity at room temperature, are pulled in bundles of about 100 by a shared motor-generator winch to about 5x their length while warm. They are spray-cooled in the grip for about 30 s (a 3 mm band cools in about L²/α ≈ 20 s), so strain-induced crystallites lock the stretch. The now force-free bundles are baled densely (about 600 kg/m³) in shaded, covered yards at about $10/m³, about $5/kWh at about 3 Wh/kg. To discharge, a bundle is gripped again and warmed with about 45°C waste heat at a rate set by the grid frequency signal; the crystallites melt and the bundle contracts against the generator, drawing part of its work from that heat. Each stroke of about 1.5 kWh on a 30 s cycle gives about 180 kW per winch head, and about 0.3 t of rubber is handled per kWh.
value: Industrial sites with waste heat get leak-free, non-hazardous multi-week storage whose medium comes with a disposal fee and whose housing is a covered bale yard instead of steel racks.
estimate: Strain-crystallizing tyre rubber stretched to about 4-5x its length stores about 10-15 kJ/kg, and after about 25% hysteresis about 3 Wh/kg comes back. So each kWh needs about 300 kg of bands, and every other cost must stay under about $0.03 per kg of rubber to reach about $10/kWh. Racks that hold the stretch need about 2 kg of steel per kg of rubber (10 MPa band stress over a 5x length, vs 200 MPa steel), about $600/kWh. A shed at about $100/m³ with racks packed at 300 kg/m³ adds about $100/kWh, so the housing is 10-60x too expensive. Cost scales as (housing $/kg)/(Wh/kg). Because locked bands carry no force, housing can drop to the price of a bale yard.

label: ED:EC:EB:g2_imm
name: Paper-machine cellophane spiral cartridges
anchor: Paper-machine laminate wound into oversized spiral cartridges
mech: A paper machine lays carbon-paper electrodes on both faces of a ~30 µm regenerated-cellulose film in one pass. The laminate is wound with mesh spacers into short spiral rolls stacked like coins in a mass-produced pressure tube. Each roll is ~6 cm tall and collected along both end faces, because 0.3 Ω/sq carbon paper at 30 A/m² already loses 20 mV over 6.7 cm. The electrolytes carry fast outer-sphere redox polymers (for example TEMPO and viologen polymers) far above the film's size cutoff, so the film holds them back about a thousandfold while small salt ions pass freely. As a result, crossover is ~0.3 A/m² against a 30 A/m² operating current (~1%) without any ion-exchange membrane or catalyst. Each m² of laminate gives ~30 W, and spent rolls are re-pulped to recover the carbon.
value: Flow-battery builders get a converter that costs about as much as paper and cellophane (~$70/kW if the laminate costs ~$2/m², assumed) and separates the electrolytes as well as a membrane, which removes the stack cost that dominates long-duration storage.
estimate: A 50 µm porous cellulose sheet lets 1 M of small redox ions through (D_eff ≈ 1.5e-10 m²/s after porosity and tortuosity) at F·D·c/L ≈ 290 A/m². That is about three times the ~100 A/m² an oversized cell carries, so most of the charge would cross the separator. The scaling law is that the crossover fraction F·D·c/(L·i) times the ohmic fraction i·L/(σ·V) is fixed at F·D·c/(σ·V) ≈ 0.0024 (σ ≈ 20 S/m, V ≈ 1 V) whatever the thickness or current, so oversizing (lower i) makes crossover worse and only the diffusivity ratio of active species to salt ions can move it. A 30 µm regenerated-cellulose (cellophane) film with redox polymers of tens of kDa (D_eff ≈ 1e-13 m²/s, assumed) gives ~0.3 A/m² of crossover, ~1% of a 30 A/m² current, with under 1 mV of separator drop.

label: ED:EC:EB:g2_evo2
name: Dilute sand-pit bipolar stack
anchor: Charge formed in place in conductive sand, behind a plain-sand diffusion barrier
mech: A lined pit holds stacked layers between bipolar carbon sheets. Each layer has ~0.15 m of carbon-coated conductive sand against each sheet, where the soluble charged species form and stay, and a ~0.13 m plain-sand barrier in between. The brine carries only 0.2 M active species in ~4 M NaCl, so conductivity stays ≈5 S/m in the sand while the force driving crossover drops five-fold. That gives ~0.06 A/m² of leak against a 1.7 A/m² one-week discharge, about 0.5% of stored charge per day, with ~8% ohmic loss each way. Each 0.43 m layer stores ~0.34 kWh per m² of sheet (~0.8 kWh per m³ of pit), and ~20 layers in a 10 m pit make a ~25 V series stack.
value: Grid operators get membrane-free storage that holds charge through multi-week lulls (~15% loss per month), with both the energy and power parts built from earthworks, sand, salt brine and carbon sheet.
estimate: With 1 M active species, D_eff ≈ 2e-10 m²/s in sand and a 0.1 m barrier, the two species leak toward each other at 2F·D_eff·c/L ≈ 0.39 A/m². That is ~2.7%/day of the 1.3e6 C/m² stored for a 5-day discharge at 3 A/m², so about half the charge is gone in a month instead of holding for months (~5x off). The scaling law is that daily loss × ohmic fraction ≈ 2F·D_eff·c·(1 day)·(L+h)/(σ_eff·V·L·t_d), so barrier thickness L only trades one loss for the other. Only lowering c while keeping σ with supporting salt, or lengthening the discharge, closes the gap. With 0.2 M active species in ~4 M NaCl (σ_eff ≈ 5 S/m), L = 0.13 m, 0.15 m conductive zones and a 1.7 A/m² one-week discharge, the leak is ~0.06 A/m² (~0.5%/day) and the ohmic loss ~8%.

label: ED:EC:EB:g1_genius
name: Shallow self-sorting electrolyte pond
anchor: Single electrolyte that sorts itself by density, with dipped electrodes
mech: A shallow lined pond about 0.4 m deep holds one membraneless electrolyte with 0.3 M of the reactant pair in a strong supporting salt, with a carbon mesh on the floor and one at the surface. Charging makes a dense oxidized form that pools on the floor and a light reduced form that floats. Discharged fluid rises or sinks by its own buoyancy into a permanent 0.25 m spent middle layer that keeps the two apart. Because ohmic drop grows with depth squared, the discharge time fixes the depth: at 3 A/m² for one week, ohmic loss is ~5%, leak ~8% and idle loss ~1%/day, so charging is still timed by the weather forecast. The pond is split into ~3 m cells wired in series so the sideways drop in each mesh stays near 30 mV, giving ~0.6 kWh and ~3.6 W per m² of pond.
value: Grid operators can cover week-long lulls with a shallow lined pond holding one liquid and two meshes per cell, with no membranes, pumps or tanks.
estimate: A 5 m pit of 1 M electrolyte stores F·c·H/2 ≈ 2.4e8 C per m² of footprint, so a one-week discharge needs ~400 A/m² through 5 m of brine (σ ≈ 20 S/m). That is ~100 V of ohmic drop against a ~1.2 V cell, roughly 1000x too much. The scaling law is that the drop, F·c·H²/(2σ·t_d), grows with depth squared, while leak across a middle buffer of thickness L is 2F·D·c/L (D ≈ 1e-9 m²/s). With H ≈ 0.4 m, c = 0.3 M, a permanent 0.25 m spent middle layer and 3 A/m², the ohmic loss is ~5% and the leak (0.23 A/m²) is ~8% of the current.

label: ED:EC:EB:g1_core
name: Layered magnetite tailings in mine voids
anchor: Buried magnetite ore used in place as solid electrodes
mech: The solid-state iron-oxide chemistry stays the same: in carbonate-buffered alkaline brine, magnetite oxidizes to maghemite/hematite on one side and reduces to ferrous hydroxide on the other, and nothing dissolves. The lens-to-lens ion path is replaced with fine magnetite tailings laid in a flooded mine void as 2 cm beds, separated by 1 cm sand layers and stacked between bipolar graphite sheets. With a ~3 cm ion path at ~5 S/m, a 10% loss of the 0.37 V allows ~5 A/m² (~2 W/m²). At an assumed 20% use of the 28 Wh/kg theoretical capacity, the ~120 kg/m² of ore per cell stores ~0.7 kWh/m²: about two weeks of discharge for ~$7/kWh of graphite sheet (assumed $5/m²). The charged ferrous side sits ~0.16 V below the hydrogen line, so its slow hydrogen-releasing decay sets the true holding time and must be measured first.
value: Owners of flooded iron mines and tailings dumps gain a non-polluting store with two-week discharge, built from waste ore, sand and carbon sheet.
estimate: Formation free energies put the hematite/magnetite and magnetite/ferrous-hydroxide couples only ~0.37 V apart, so 100 MW needs ~2.7e8 A. Holding ohmic loss to 10% then needs under ~1.4e-10 Ω, which through 30 m of brine-filled rock (σ ≈ 0.1 S/m) means ~2e12 m² of facing lens area. A real 1 km² lens pair carries ~1e-4 A/m², about 50 W in total, so the design falls short by ~10^6. The length of the ion path between the lenses controls the power, not the mineral surface area. That path cannot be shortened in place, because two electrodes inside one conductive ore body short-circuit.

label: ED:EC:EB:g1_loop2
name: Pickle-liquor electrolyte refining cascade
anchor: Stepped-potential cascade that identifies couples in waste brine by charge counting
mech: Iron-rich industrial waste brine, mainly spent steel pickle liquor (~120 g/L iron as FeCl2), flows through a cascade of cheap cells held at stepped potentials. At each stage, the charge passed minus the measured conversion shows which couple the stage is working on. Stages that find parasitic metals such as zinc, nickel or copper plate or precipitate them out. The iron leaves as purified flow-battery electrolyte at ~30,000 m³ per GWh, so one pickling line (~100 m³/day) yields ~1 GWh of storage electrolyte a year. Liquor-disposal fees pay for the cascade, dilute mine drainage (~0.2 g/L, 600x leaner) is limited to remediation work, and new stack area is added only where measured charge return justifies it.
value: Steelmakers turn a hazardous waste they pay to dispose of into ~1 GWh/yr of purified iron electrolyte per pickling line, and nearby grids get storage electrolyte whose purification is paid for by waste treatment.
estimate: An all-iron flow battery (~1.2 V) needs ~3.5 kg of iron per kWh (31 mol of electrons, 47 mol Fe at ~70% use), i.e. ~3500 t per GWh. A large acid-mine discharge (50 L/s at 200 mg/L Fe) carries only ~300 t/yr, which means ~11 years and ~1.7e7 m³ of water per GWh. Electrolyte supply, not the stack, therefore limits the claim. The controlling ratio is the iron concentration of the feed: spent steel pickle liquor (~120 g/L Fe, assumed, about 600x richer) needs only ~30,000 m³ per GWh, so one pickling line making ~100 m³/day supplies ~1 GWh of electrolyte per year.

label: ED:EC:EB:g1_loop
name: Cavern-fed buffered biphasic trays
anchor: Cavern brine/organic store stratified by charge, feeding membraneless trays
mech: A salt cavern stores a dense brine carrying one cheap redox couple beneath an immiscible organic liquid carrying the other. It is stratified by state of charge, so metres of spent liquid at the interface hold the bulk leak to ~0.04 A/m² (5 m buffer, 1 M). At the surface the liquids run through stacked shallow trays between plain carbon plates. The brine enters as two side-by-side flowing laminae: charged brine against the bottom plate, and a ≥1.5 mm lamina of spent brine from the cavern interface zone against the 1 mm organic layer. With 2-min residence, charged brine molecules cannot cross the spent lamina (√(Dt) ≈ 0.35 mm), so interfacial leak is ~1% of the current at 40 A/m². The highly conductive brine buffer adds only ~3 mV, while the organic layer costs ~0.1 V.
value: Grid operators get multi-week storage at the gigawatt-hour scale with no membrane or tank, where a spent-liquid buffer in both the cavern and each tray keeps self-discharge near one percent.
estimate: During discharge both tray layers arrive fully charged, so the two charged species meet at the liquid–liquid interface. If electron transfer there is fast (as for ferrocene/ferricyanide), the leak is limited only by diffusion, at ≈2F·c·√(D/πt) ≈ 260 A/m² over a 3-min stay (c = 1 M, D = 1e-9 m²/s). That is several times the ≤50 A/m² that the ohmic drop of the 1 mm organic layer (σ ≈ 0.4 S/m) allows. The controlling length is a spent buffer s at the interface compared with √(D·t) ≈ 0.35 mm, since leak falls as exp(−s²/4Dt). A 1.5 mm spent-brine lamina with 2-min residence cuts the leak to ~0.0007 mol/m² per pass, ~1.3% of the 0.05 mol/m² moved at 40 A/m².

label: ED:EC:EB:g1_genius
name: Honeycomb solar-pond electrochemical cells
anchor: Solar-pond heated electrolytes separated by a salt step
mech: A lined solar pond keeps a metre-thick salt gradient on top as a heat trap, so the bottom zone runs at ~70 °C. Inside it, a dense 1 M charged electrolyte ~0.7 m deep lies beneath a lighter one, separated by a 0.1 m salt step with carbon meshes just above and below it, and convection in each warm layer carries reactants to the meshes. Thin plastic honeycomb walls through the full depth divide the pond into ~0.8 m cells, and each cell's upper mesh is wired in series to the next cell's lower mesh. Each mesh then carries only ~24 A and loses ~30 mV, and the walls block shunt currents. At ~38 A/m² this gives ~10% leak, ~10% ohmic loss, ~0.5% of charge lost per idle day, and ~23 kWh and ~45 W per m² of pond. Heat raises leak and conductivity about equally, so its real gain is faster electrode kinetics.
value: Grid operators get three-week electrochemical storage built from a salt pond, carbon mesh and a plastic honeycomb, with free solar heat speeding the electrodes and no tanks, membranes or pumps.
estimate: At ~70 °C (D ≈ 2e-9 m²/s, σ ≈ 30 S/m), a 0.1 m step leaks 2F·D·c/L ≈ 3.9 A/m² at 1 M. Running at ~38 A/m² therefore balances ~10% leak against ~10% ohmic loss, with ~0.7 m layers for a three-week discharge, so the electrochemistry passes. But a pond-wide mesh must carry that current sideways: the drop is ≈ i·R_s·W²/8 ≈ 475 V across a 100 m pond with a 0.01 Ω/sq graphite mesh, against ~0.03 V allowed. Pond width, not depth or step thickness, controls the limit, and W must be ≤ ~0.8 m.

label: g3_law1
name: Centimetre Iron-Manganese Slabs
mech: Alkaline iron anode slabs and MnO₂ cathode slabs, each about 3 cm thick and filled with coke, sit in 12 S/m KOH across a single separator. The slab thickness is chosen from the 250-hour discharge time, since the ion-conduction length grows with the square root of time. The result stores about 1 V per electron pair, using roughly 1 kg Fe and 3 kg MnO₂ per kWh.
value: About 50× less collector and separator per kWh, with materials near $8/kWh, makes ten-day storage cheap.

label: g3_law1
name: Sand-Gapped Polymer Flow Cell
mech: Lignin-derived quinone macromolecules (D ≈ 1e-13) in 4 M NaCl flow on both sides of a centimetre-wide bed of packed sand, with no membrane. Crossover fraction times ohmic fraction is fixed at about 5e-7, so 0.5% resistive loss comes with only 0.01% crossover. Capacity scales with tank volume.
value: It removes the costliest flow-battery part, the ion-exchange membrane, while keeping crossover negligible.

label: g3_law1
name: Spent-Sheath Iron-Chromium Flow
mech: The charged Fe³⁺ stream and the charged Cr²⁺ stream run side by side down a cheap plastic channel. A 1.5 mm sheath of their own discharged mixed electrolyte separates them, and they stay in contact for about two minutes. Diffusive leak through the sheath falls as exp(−s²/4Dt), to about 1%, while ions conduct across it with only about 10 mV of loss.
value: An iron-chromium flow battery with no membrane and chemicals near $10/kWh.

label: g3_law2
name: Poured-slab multi-day electrodes
mech: Iron-oxide paste and manganese-ore paste, each made conductive with coke, are cast in centimetre-thick layers with a KOH gel between them, in cheap trays. A 100-hour discharge lets ions cross 1.5 cm of electrode, so foil, separator and housing per kWh drop about 50x. Bi₂S₃ added to the iron layer suppresses hydrogen evolution during weeks of holding.
value: Batteries stamped out like concrete paving, at under $10/kWh, sized for week-long lulls.

label: g3_law2
name: Three-lamina falling-film cell
mech: Charged ferric chloride, spent ferrous chloride and an iron-plating wall share one membraneless gap that the liquids fall through. The 1.5 mm spent middle layer gives charged species too little time to diffuse across it. A splitter at the bottom separates the streams back into their tanks.
value: Membrane-free flow storage that uses only iron salt as the medium.

label: g3_law2
name: Sand-divided dilute-brine flow cell
mech: Dilute iron and chromium chlorides (0.2 M) ride in concentrated sodium chloride brine, which carries most of the current. Because the salt is much more mobile than the actives, a plain sand layer keeps crossover and resistance both near 2%. The same mixed electrolyte is stored in lined ponds on both sides.
value: Flow storage at about $12/kWh using only commodity salt, iron, chromium and sand.

label: ELD:g3_law1
name: Silica-flour membraneless quinone cell
anchor: Membraneless mineral bed between quinone brines
mech: Lignin-derived quinone electrolytes in 4 M NaCl flow on both sides of a 0.2-mm layer of 1-µm silica flour on a coarse-sand backing, with no membrane. Leak through a porous bed is set by grain size, not thickness. At a permeability of about 1e-15 m², a 10 Pa imbalance between the sides leaks under 1% of the current, and mirrored low-pressure-drop flow-by channels keep the imbalance that small; diffusion adds about 1.7%. The thin layer carries about 280 A/m² at 2% resistive loss (about 170 W/m²), and capacity scales with tank volume.
value: Grid operators get flow storage with no ion-exchange membrane: cents of ground quartz per m² replace the costliest stack part, and crossover stays at a few percent.
estimate: Any pressure difference Δp across the bed drives Darcy flow u = kΔp/(μL), and the useful current is j = fσ_eff·V/L. So the ratio of convective leak to useful current, cFkΔp/(μ·f·σ_eff·V), depends on neither the bed width L nor D. Assumed numbers: 0.1-mm sand, k ≈ 1e-11 m², μ = 1.3e-3 Pa·s, c = 500 mol/m³ of electrons, σ_eff ≈ 4 S/m, V = 0.7 V, f = 0.5%. That gives a leak of about 26x the useful current per pascal, so a realistic 10-100 Pa imbalance means a leak 250-2600x the useful current (and by Stokes-Einstein, D = 1e-13 m²/s implies ~2 µm particles; real lignin macromolecules have D ≈ 1e-10). Grain size controls the leak because k ∝ d², while bed width only sets power, which is about 1 W/m² at 1 cm. Fix: 1-µm silica (k ≈ 1e-15) at f = 2% gives 6.5e-4 per Pa, about 0.7% at 10 Pa; diffusion adds DcF/(fσV) ≈ 1.7% at D = 1e-10; and a 0.2-mm layer carries about 280 A/m².

label: ELD:g3_law2
name: Tilted layered iron-salt channel
anchor: Layered membraneless all-iron liquid gap
mech: Charged ferric chloride, a 1.5-mm layer of spent ferrous chloride and an iron-plating wall share one membraneless 3-mm channel tilted only about 0.25°. The liquids creep at about 2 cm/s (Reynolds number about 40) instead of falling turbulently. The layers are stacked by density: the salted, densest ferric layer sits on a carbon floor and the plating wall forms the ceiling, where hydrogen vents. Fe³⁺ spreads only about 0.17 mm in each 50-s pass, a splitter at the outlet returns each layer to its tank, and at about 150 A/m² the cell gives about 150 W/m².
value: Utilities that need multi-day backup get membrane-free flow storage whose only active medium is iron salt.
estimate: Free fall down a vertical 3-mm gap reaches u = ρgw²/(12μ) = 1000×9.8×(3e-3)²/(12×1.5e-3) ≈ 5 m/s. That gives Re ≈ 1e4, so turbulence mixes the 1.5-mm buffer within milliseconds, and keeping free fall laminar (Re < ~100) would need a gap under about 0.65 mm. The flow speed is set by the slope that drives it, not by layer thickness. Tilting to sinθ ≈ 0.004 gives u ≈ 2 cm/s, Re ≈ 40, and 50 s over 1 m. Fe³⁺ then diffuses only √(6e-10×50) ≈ 0.17 mm, much less than 1.5 mm (leak about erfc(4.4) ≈ 1e-9), and the mass-transfer limit 2Fc√(D/πt) is about 380 A/m² at 1 M.

label: ELD:g3_law1
name: Thick-slab iron-manganese cell
anchor: Thick slabs sized by √(discharge time)
mech: An alkaline iron anode slab (about 1.5 cm) and a coke-filled MnO₂ cathode slab (about 3 cm) sit in KOH (12 S/m effective in the pores) across one separator. Ohmic drop grows as L²/t, so a 250-hour discharge lets the cathode be 3 cm thick with only about 0.09 V of drop at about 74 A/m². Each m² of separator and collector then stores about 18 kWh, using roughly 1 kg Fe and 3 kg MnO₂ per kWh at about 1 V.
value: Grids riding through calm, dark spells get ten-day storage with about 50x less collector and separator per kWh and materials near $8-15/kWh.
estimate: With uniform reaction, the ohmic drop across a slab is ΔV ≈ jL/(2σ) with j = q_v·L/t, so ΔV = q_v·L²/(2σt) and L = √(2σΔVt/q_v). MnO₂ at 40 vol% (5 g/cm³, 308 mAh/g) gives q_v ≈ 0.62 Ah/cm³ = 2.2e9 C/m³. With σ = 12 S/m, t = 9e5 s and 50 mV allowed per slab, L ≈ 2.2 cm, against 3 cm claimed (0.09 V at 74 A/m², within 2x). Iron holds about 2.3 Ah/cm³, so a 1.5-cm iron slab (about 0.05 V) is enough. The total drop is about 0.14 V on a cell of about 1 V, at about 18 kWh per m² of separator.

label: ELD:g3_law2
name: Salt-carried iron-chromium silica cell
anchor: Brine-carried current over dilute Fe/Cr actives
mech: Iron and chromium chlorides at 0.2 M are dissolved in about 4.5 M sodium chloride brine, and the brine carries the current. Between the sides, instead of a membrane, a 0.5-mm layer of 1-µm silica flour on a sand backing keeps both crossover and resistive loss near 2% at about 200 A/m². The silica's permeability of about 1e-15 m² means a 30 Pa pressure mismatch leaks only about 0.4%. The same mixed electrolyte, about 0.37 m³ per kWh, is stored in covered, lined ponds on both sides.
value: Grids needing week-scale reserves get flow storage at about $12-20/kWh, made only from commodity salt, iron, chromium and ground quartz.
estimate: Diffusion holds: crossover fraction × ohmic fraction = DcF/(σV) = 5e-10×200×96485/(22×1.18) ≈ 3.7e-4 ≈ 2%×2%, for any layer thickness. But a pressure difference drives Darcy flow, and the ratio of leak to useful current, cFkΔp/(μ·f·σ_eff·V), also does not depend on thickness. For 0.1-mm sand (k ≈ 1e-11 m², μ = 1.5e-3 Pa·s, σ_eff ≈ 4.4 S/m, f = 2%) the leak is about 1.2x the useful current per pascal, so a 10-100 Pa imbalance leaks 12-120x the useful current. Grain size controls this because k ∝ d²: 1-µm silica flour (k ≈ 1e-15) gives about 1.2e-4 per Pa, or about 0.4% at 30 Pa, and a 0.5-mm layer carries about 200 A/m².

label: ELD:g3_law1
name: Stacked self-sheathed iron-chromium channel
anchor: Self-sheathed co-flowing Fe/Cr streams
mech: The charged Fe³⁺ stream flows along a carbon floor, a 1.5-mm sheath of discharged mixed electrolyte flows above it, and the charged Cr²⁺ stream runs along a carbon ceiling, where hydrogen vents. All three move through a flat plastic channel about 1.2 m long at about 1 cm/s, giving about 2 minutes of contact. Stacking them in density order, with the bottom stream salted at least 1% denser, stops buoyant overturning. That leaves only a diffusive leak of about e^-7.8 ≈ 0.04%, while ions cross the sheath with about 5 mV of loss at about 100 A/m².
value: Multi-day grid storage from an iron-chromium flow battery with no membrane and chemicals near $10/kWh.
estimate: Diffusion is fine: s²/4Dt = (1.5e-3)²/(4×6e-10×120) ≈ 7.8, so the leak is about e^-7.8 ≈ 4e-4, and ohmic loss is about 100 A/m² × 1.5 mm / 30 S/m ≈ 5 mV. But side-by-side streams have vertical interfaces. A charged-to-discharged density difference of only 0.5% (g' ≈ 0.05 m/s²) makes them slump at about ½√(g'H) ≈ 1 cm/s in a 1-cm-deep channel, crossing the sheath in about 0.15 s instead of the 120 s needed, which is about 1000x too short. What controls the leak is how the interfaces sit relative to gravity, not sheath thickness. Stacked horizontally in stable density order, only diffusion is left, and the wall reaction limit 2Fc√(D/πt) ≈ 240 A/m² at 1 M sets about 100 A/m² as the working rate.

label: ELD:g3_law2
name: Paved iron-manganese ore trays
anchor: Cast tray layers of iron/manganese-ore paste
mech: Iron-oxide paste (with Bi₂S₃ against hydrogen evolution) and manganese-ore paste, both made conductive with coke, are cast about 1.5 cm thick in cheap trays. Between them is a KOH gel layer about 1.2 cm thick that also serves as a water reservoir. Discharging consumes 0.67 kg of water per kWh, and the gel holds about 2.6 kg/kWh, so the electrolyte only goes from 7 M to about 9.5 M. A 100-hour discharge at about 75 A/m² crosses each layer with about 0.06 V of drop, storing about 7.5 kWh per m² of tray.
value: Utilities facing week-long calm, dark spells get batteries stamped out like concrete paving at roughly $10/kWh.
estimate: Discharge (Fe + 2MnO₂ + 2H₂O → Fe(OH)₂ + 2MnOOH) consumes one water molecule per electron: 1 kWh at about 1 V is 37 mol e⁻, or 0.67 kg of water. Assume a 1.5-cm ore cathode at about 0.5 Ah/cm³, giving 7.5 kWh/m² or 0.13 m² per kWh. With about 35% pores plus a 3-mm gel, the tray holds only about 1.4 L of 7 M KOH (about 1.2 kg of water). A full discharge then removes about 55% of the water and pushes KOH to about 14 M, near saturation, with conductivity roughly halved. The controlling ratio is water held per kWh against 0.67 kg, not electrode thickness; ohmic drop at 100 h is fine at about 75 A/m² × 1.5 cm / (2 × 10 S/m) ≈ 0.06 V. A gel reservoir about 1.2 cm thick raises the water to about 2.6 kg/kWh, so KOH only swings from 7 to 9.5 M, at an extra ~30 mV and under $1/kWh of KOH.
